﴿Why do you say what you do not do?﴾ Regarding its occasion of revelation (*sabab al-nuzul*), there are three opinions. The first is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas: a group of people said, "We wish we knew the most beloved of deeds to Allah so that we might do it." So Allah prescribed jihad, but some people disliked it, and the verse was revealed. The second is that some young men among the Muslims used to speak of themselves in regard to military expedition (*ghazw*) with things they had not done, saying, "We did this and we did that," and that was a lie, so the verse was revealed to rebuke them. The third is that it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, because they used to say to the believers, "We are with you and of you," and then their actions would show the opposite. This last opinion is weak, because the verse addresses them with His words, ﴿O you who have believed﴾, unless it is meant that they believed according to their own claim and in what they displayed.

Despite this, the ruling of the verse is general in rebuking whoever says what he does not do. ﴿Greatly hateful it is in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do.﴾ Some of the early generations (*salaf*) were too shy to admonish people because of this verse, saying, "I fear the hatred of Allah." *Al-maqt* is aversion (*al-bughd*) due to a blameworthy matter or the like. The word *maqtan* is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyiz*), and *an taqulu* is the subject (*fa'il*) of *kabura*. It is also said that the subject of *kabura* is an omitted noun, its meaning being: "Your action has become greatly hateful, *maqtan*, and *an taqulu* is a substitute (*badal*) for the omitted subject, or the predicate of an implied inceptive subject."

﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in ranks (*saffan*), as if they were a solid structure.﴾ The occurrence of this verse here is evidence that the verse before it concerns fighting. Some people said: infantry fighting is superior to cavalry fighting, because the closing of ranks (*al-tarras*) is more achievable in it than for horsemen. This was said by Ibn 'Atiyya, but it is weak; the one who said it missed the purpose of the verse. The intended meaning is not the closing of ranks itself, but steadfastness and earnestness in fighting.

﴿As if they were a solid structure (*bunyan marsus*).﴾ *Al-marsus* is that which is joined together, one part to another. It is also said that it is that which is bound with lead (*al-rasas*), and it is not far-fetched that this is the original meaning of the word.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 61, verse 5:

﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, why do you hurt me, when you know that I am the Messenger of Allah to you?" But when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate.﴾

They used to harm him with bad speech, disobey him, and belittle him. And see in al-Ahzab ﴿Do not be like those who hurt Moses﴾ [al-Ahzab: 69]. ﴿And you know that I am the Messenger of Allah to you﴾: this is the establishment of proof against them and a rebuke to them, and a condemnation of harming him despite their knowledge that he is the Messenger of Allah. For this reason, qad (قد), which indicates certainty (tahqiq), was introduced. ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾: this is a punishment for a sin with a sin, and zayagh al-qalb (زيغ القلب, the deviation of the heart) is its inclination away from the truth.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 61, verses 6–7:

﴿And when Jesus, son of Mary, said: "O Children of Israel, indeed I am the messenger of Allah to you, confirming what is before me of the Torah"﴾ Musa said "O my people," while Isa said "O Children of Israel," because he had no father among them.

﴿Confirming what is before me of the Torah﴾: its meaning has been mentioned in Surat al-Ahzab [33:41], in His saying, "confirming what is with you."

﴿And giving good tidings of a messenger﴾: on the authority of Ka'b (al-Ahbar), that the disciples (al-Hawariyyun) said to Isa: "O Spirit of Allah, is there any nation after us?" He said: "Yes, the nation of Ahmad: wise, learned, pious, and righteous."

﴿Whose name is Ahmad﴾: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I have five names: I am Muhammad, I am Ahmad, I am al-Mahi (the Eraser) through whom Allah erases disbelief, I am al-Hashir (the Gatherer) at whose feet people will be gathered, and I am al-Aqib (the Last), after whom there is no prophet."

Ahmad is derived from al-hamd (praise). It may be a verb by which he was named, or an adjective by which he was named, like Ahmad. It may also mean "one who praises" (hamid) or "one who is praised" (mahmud), like Muhammad.

﴿And when he came to them with the clear proofs﴾: it may refer to Isa or to Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon them both. The first interpretation is supported by its connection to what precedes it, and the second by His saying, "while he is being called to Islam," since the one who calls to Islam is Muhammad ﷺ.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 61, verses 11–13:

﴿You believe in Allah﴾: this clause is an explanation of the trade mentioned (the commerce that is named in the preceding verse). Al-Akhfash said: it is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to it.

﴿He will forgive you your sins﴾: it is in the jussive (jazm) as the answer (jawab) to "you believe" (tu'minun), because it carries the meaning of a command. Ibn Mas'ud recited it as "Believe in Allah and strive (amanu wa-jahidu)" in the imperative form, because the imperative implies urging (tahdid).

﴿And another [favour] you love﴾: "another" (ukhra) is in the nominative (irtafaʿa) by being a subject of an elided beginning, whose estimated meaning is: "and for you is another favour." Or it is in the accusative (intasaba) as an object of an elided verb, whose estimated meaning is: "and He will grant you another."

﴿Help from Allah and an imminent victory﴾: this is an explanation of "another," so it is a substitute (badal) for it.

﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾: al-Zamakhshari said: it is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "you believe in Allah," because it has the meaning of a command.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 61, verse 14:

﴿Be the helpers of Allah﴾. Ansar is the plural of nasir (helper), and the name al-Ansar has become predominantly applied to the Aws and the Khazraj; Allah named them by it, but that is not the meaning intended here. ﴿As Isa, son of Maryam, said﴾. This comparison is to be understood in terms of meaning, because its apparent sense would be: "Be the helpers of Allah as Isa said." The meaning is: "Be the helpers of Allah as the disciples (al-Hawariyyun) said when Isa said to them: 'Who are my helpers in the way of Allah?'" The meaning of al-Hawariyyun and "my helpers in the way of Allah" has already been mentioned in Al 'Imran [52]. ﴿So they became dominant﴾. It has been said: they became dominant through proof (bi'l-hujjah). It has also been said: they overcame the disbelievers through fighting after Isa (peace be upon him) was raised. And it has been said: the dominance of the believers among them was through Muhammad (ﷺ).
